title: Theodicies Steelmanned
subtitle: The free-will defense, soul-making, skeptical theism, and the cross-centered and protest responses. Each at its strongest.
triageNote: That God is good and not the author of evil is first-order, and every response on this page is trying to defend it. What runs lower, and divides thoughtful believers, is which account of why God permits evil actually holds, and whether any explanation should be attempted at all. Some Christians build careful theodicies; others think the whole project of explaining suffering is a mistake and answer only with the cross or with honest protest. That disagreement is real and runs between faithful people who all kneel at the same cross. Hold the goodness of God tightly. Hold your particular theodicy with a light hand, and never offer any of them to a sufferer as though it settled their grief, because an explanation and a comfort are not the same thing.
question: Grant that the existence of God and the existence of evil are not flatly contradictory, that the logical problem can be answered. A harder question remains. Can we say anything, even tentatively, about why a good and all-powerful God permits the suffering we see, or at least show that he might have a reason worth the cost. A theodicy is an attempt to do exactly that, to justify the ways of God in the face of evil, and over the centuries several have been built, each serious, each defended by careful minds. The free-will defense says the great good of genuine freedom required the possibility of its abuse. The soul-making theodicy says a world with suffering is the only kind that can grow real souls. Skeptical theism says we are in no position to judge whether God has good reasons we cannot see. And a different kind of response, the cross-centered and the protest traditions, says the whole project of explanation is a mistake, that the right answer to evil is not a theory but a God who suffers and a lament that refuses to make peace with the horror. This page lays each out at its strongest, with the author hidden, and asks which, if any, can carry the weight. The test is not only whether an answer is logically sound. It is whether it can be said out loud at a graveside without becoming a lie.
whyItMatters:
A theodicy is not an abstract exercise, because you will reach for one, or refuse to, in the worst moment of someone's life, and the one you reach for will either help or wound. The person who has only the free-will defense will say to a grieving parent that the price of human freedom is sometimes a child's death, which is true in a way and unspeakable in the moment. The person who has only soul-making will tell the sufferer their agony is making them a better person, which can sound like God is using their child's death as a teaching tool. The person who has only skeptical theism will say God surely has a reason we cannot see, which is honest but can land as a shrug. Knowing the theodicies, and knowing where each one helps and where each one becomes cruel, is the difference between a comfort and a fresh injury. This is pastoral knowledge before it is philosophical knowledge.

It matters, too, because the theodicies are not interchangeable, and they cost different things. Some of them, to get God off the hook, quietly limit his sovereignty or imply that the suffering was really fine all along, and those costs are theological, not just emotional. Part of weighing a theodicy is asking what it has to give up about God in order to work. A theodicy that solves the problem by making God smaller, or by making evil less than evil, has not solved the problem. It has changed the subject.

And it matters because of a deep disagreement among faithful Christians that this page cannot dodge: whether you should attempt a theodicy at all. A whole tradition holds that the project is misguided, that to explain suffering is already to betray it, and that the only faithful responses are the lament that protests and the cross that shares. Another tradition holds that we owe people some account of how a good God and a wracked world fit together, or faith looks like willful blindness. Where you stand on that question shapes everything you will say in the dark, and it is worth knowing the strongest case for each before you decide.

positions.name: The free-will defense
positions.inOneLine: Genuine moral good requires creatures who are genuinely free, freedom necessarily includes the possibility of choosing evil, and a world with free creatures who sometimes sin is better than a world of puppets who cannot, so God's permitting evil is the price of a greater good.
positions.bestCase:
Start with what God was after, because the defense turns on the value of the thing risked. God did not want a universe of machines that always behave. He wanted creatures who could love him and one another freely, and love that is not free is not love at all, it is mechanism wearing love's face. A wife who embraces you only because she is programmed to has not loved you. So if God wanted the genuine good of free love, free worship, free moral action, he had to make creatures who could really choose, and a creature who can really choose the good is, by the same power, a creature who can choose evil. You cannot have the one capacity without the other. The possibility of evil is the shadow cast by the great good of freedom.

Now let me be precise, because my version is modest and that is its strength. I am not claiming to know that this is in fact why God permits each evil. I am answering the charge that God and evil are contradictory, and for that I only need to show that it is possible that God could not bring about the good of free creatures without permitting the evil they might do. Alvin Plantinga sharpened this against the claim that an omnipotent God could simply have made free creatures who always freely choose good. His answer, the famous one, is that for all we know it may be that every possible free creature, in every world God could make, would go wrong at some point, a condition he called transworld depravity. If that is even possibly true, then it is possibly the case that a world with free creatures and some evil is the best God could do without abolishing freedom, and the alleged contradiction collapses. I do not have to prove transworld depravity is actual. I only have to show it is possible, and no one has shown it impossible.

What about the suffering that no free choice causes, the disease, the earthquake. Here I extend the defense rather than abandon it. Perhaps a world stable enough for free creatures to act in, with reliable natural laws they can understand and use, necessarily contains the possibility of those laws causing harm, fire that warms and also burns, water that sustains and also drowns. And the older tradition added that some natural evil may trace to the free rebellion of spiritual powers, a fallen creation, which keeps even natural evil within the orbit of misused freedom. I grant these extensions are more speculative than the core. But the core stands firm: the greatest goods, love and goodness freely given, require a freedom that can be abused, and a God who wanted those goods had reason to permit the abuse. That is not a cold calculation. It is the same logic by which any parent lets a child grow up free enough to break their heart, because the alternative, a child who cannot choose, is no child at all.
advocates: C. S. Lewis (The Problem of Pain)
much of the broad theistic tradition

positions.name: The soul-making theodicy
positions.inOneLine: God's purpose is not to make a comfortable world but to grow mature souls, and the virtues that make a person great, courage, compassion, perseverance, love, can only be formed in a world that contains real hardship, so suffering is the necessary environment of the soul's making.
positions.bestCase:
Ask the wrong question and you will never understand this world. The wrong question is, why did a good God not make a comfortable paradise. The right question is, what kind of world would a good God make if his goal were not our comfort but our greatness, the formation of mature, virtuous, God-loving souls. And once you ask that, the world we have starts to make a different kind of sense. I draw this from Irenaeus, the second-century bishop, who read the creation of humanity not as a finished perfection that fell, but as a beginning, an immature creature placed in a difficult world to grow up into the likeness of God. John Hick gave this its modern shape, and called it soul-making, borrowing the phrase from the poet Keats, who called the world a vale of soul-making.

Here is the heart of it. The virtues we most admire, the ones that make a human soul beautiful, cannot exist in a world without hardship. Courage is impossible without danger. Compassion is impossible without suffering to be moved by. Perseverance, patience, sacrificial love, forgiveness, all of them require a world where things are hard, where there is something to endure, someone to forgive, a cost to be paid. A frictionless paradise could produce pleasant creatures, but it could never produce a courageous one or a compassionate one, because there would be nothing to be brave about and no one to have mercy on. So if God's aim is souls of real depth and real virtue, formed freely through their own struggle rather than stamped out ready-made, then a world with genuine difficulty is not a failure of his goodness. It is the instrument of it. The Bible says exactly this more often than we notice: that suffering produces endurance, endurance character, character hope; that we are disciplined as sons; that the trying of faith works patience.

I know the hardest objection and I will face it. There is suffering that seems to make no soul, that destroys rather than refines, the child who dies before any growth, the trauma that breaks a person rather than building them. I do not pretend this is easy. My answer has two parts. First, that the soul-making world must be genuinely lawlike and genuinely risky, or the growth would be fake, which means the same conditions that allow growth allow catastrophe, and you cannot have a world safe enough to prevent all tragedy that is still demanding enough to make real souls. Second, and this is why the theodicy needs more than this life to work, that the soul-making is not finished at death. Hick held that God's patient work of forming the soul continues beyond the grave, so that no life is finally wasted and no suffering is ultimately for nothing, because the One who began the making will complete it. Without that hope the theodicy fails, and I admit it. With it, the vale of tears becomes what it was always meant to be, the hard country where God grows his children up.
advocates: John Hick (Evil and the God of Love)
strands of the Eastern and Wesleyan traditions

positions.name: Skeptical theism
positions.inOneLine: Given the vast gap between God's wisdom and ours, we are in no position to judge that the suffering we see is genuinely pointless, so the inference from this looks pointless to so there is probably no good reason fails, and the believer need not produce a theodicy to be rational.
positions.bestCase:
I want to answer the evidential problem without the burden the other theodicies carry, and I do it by questioning a single hidden assumption in the objection. The evidential argument runs: this suffering appears pointless, therefore it probably is pointless, therefore probably no good God permits it. Watch the move in the middle, from appears pointless to is pointless. That inference is only as good as your confidence that if there were a good reason, you would be able to see it. And that is exactly the confidence I deny we have any right to.

Consider the gap. If God exists, he is infinitely wise, sees the whole web of causes and consequences down every corridor of time, weighs goods and connections we cannot even name. We are creatures of a moment, who cannot reliably predict next week, who routinely discover years later that some hardship we cursed was the hinge of everything good that followed. Now, given that gap, how confident should you be that you can survey a particular instance of suffering and correctly judge that there is no good reason God could have for permitting it, no good reason anywhere in the whole tapestry of providence. I say your confidence should be near zero, because the situation is exactly like a child watching a surgeon cut into her parent and concluding the surgeon is cruel. The child sees the knife and the blood and not the reason, and the child is in no position to judge, not because she is stupid, but because the relevant knowledge is beyond her. We are that child before God's reasons. This is what William Alston and Stephen Wykstra argued: we have no good grounds for thinking that the goods we can detect are a representative sample of the goods there are. So the suffering looks pointless. Of course it does. That is exactly what we should expect even if every instance had a point, given how little of the whole we can see.

Notice what I am not claiming, because my modesty is my strength. I am not claiming to know the reasons. I am not offering a theodicy at all. I am refusing to draw the atheist's conclusion from premises that do not support it. The atheist needs me to be able to see that there is no good reason, and I am simply pointing out that, given the kind of creature I am and the kind of God this would be, I could never be in a position to see that, so the absence of a visible reason is no evidence at all. The objection requires a vantage point none of us has. Some say this leaves the believer with cold comfort, and they are right that it is not warm. It is not meant to be warm. It is meant to be true, and to free the believer from the false demand that she explain what she was never in a position to explain. Job got no reasons either, and was not faulted for lacking them.
advocates: much of recent analytic defense of theism

positions.name: The cross-centered and protest responses
positions.inOneLine: The attempt to explain or justify suffering is itself a mistake that betrays the sufferer, and the only faithful responses are the cross, where God shares the suffering rather than explaining it, and lament, which protests the evil before God rather than making peace with it.
positions.bestCase:
Let me say what the other three have in common, because it is the thing I most distrust. Each of them, however carefully, ends by giving suffering a justification, a point, a place in a system where it turns out to be, on balance, acceptable. And I think that move, the move that makes any particular horror finally all right, is a betrayal. Stand at the bed of a dying child and try to say the words the free-will defense or the soul-making theodicy would have you say, and you will hear it: the explanation, in that room, becomes obscene. Ivan Karamazov saw this. He did not deny God exists. He said that even if every tear is one day wiped away and every cruelty woven into some final harmony, he would respectfully return the ticket, because no future harmony can be worth the torture of a single child, and a God who asks you to accept that the torture was worth it is asking too much. I think Ivan is closer to the heart of the gospel than the theodicists, because he refuses to call the evil anything but evil.

So what is the faithful response, if not explanation. Two things, and the Bible is full of both. The first is lament, the protest the Psalms make and the church has largely forgotten how to make: How long, O Lord? Why do you hide your face? My God, why have you forsaken me? Lament does not explain suffering and does not make peace with it. It hauls the suffering into the presence of God and refuses to be quiet, and Scripture not only permits this, it models it, gives us the words, includes a whole book of Lamentations and a Psalm 88 that ends in darkness. The faithful sufferer is not the one who finds the reason. It is the one who keeps talking to God, angrily if need be, instead of explaining God to herself.

The second is the cross, and this is everything. The Christian God does not answer the problem of evil from a safe distance, with a theory. He answers it by entering the evil himself. The God you are tempted to put on trial is the God who was tortured by Roman nails, abandoned, and killed, who cried the exact cry of every godforsaken sufferer, my God, why have you forsaken me, and got no answer in the moment either. Bonhoeffer, writing from a prison cell before the Nazis hanged him, said only the suffering God can help. Not a God who explains your suffering, but a God who has wounds. That does not tell you why your child died. It tells you that when she died, God was not the comfortable spectator the objection imagines. He was the one who knows, from the inside, what it is to scream into a silent sky. And then a promise, that the crucified one rose, and that the suffering is real but not final, and that the proper response to evil now is not to justify it but to fight it, mourn it, and wait for the God who entered it to finish what the empty tomb began. I would rather give a sufferer that than the best theodicy ever written, because the theodicy makes peace with the horror, and the cross declares war on it.
advocates: the lament tradition of the Psalms

biblicalEvidence.summary: God gives the man a real command with a real alternative, and the humans freely choose to disobey. The story places a genuine choice, with genuine stakes, at the origin of human evil, and the evil enters through the misuse of freedom.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes evil simply God's doing, since the narrative locates the entry of evil in a free creaturely choice against a clear command.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The free-will defense reads this as the paradigm: God risks real freedom, and evil enters through its abuse, not through any defect in God's making. The soul-making view reads the same story as the beginning of a maturing process, humanity placed in a world where it must grow. The protest and cross-centered view notes that the story explains the origin of evil without justifying any particular present horror, and that Scripture quickly moves from explanation to lament.

biblicalEvidence.summary: We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope. Paul traces a chain in which suffering is the soil of mature character and hope.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a view that suffering is sheer waste, since Paul makes it productive of endurance, character, and hope; and pressed against any reading that suffering is therefore always good, since Paul speaks of rejoicing in it by faith, not pretending it is not painful.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The soul-making theodicy reads this as its charter: suffering forms the soul. The protest and cross-centered view answers that Paul speaks of his own sufferings for the gospel, freely embraced, not of a parent told their child's death is character-building, and warns against turning a first-person testimony into a third-person explanation imposed on others' grief. The free-will defense reads it as one of the goods that can come from a world where suffering is possible.

biblicalEvidence.summary: My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts. The gap between divine and human understanding is stated directly.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any confident claim that we can survey God's reasons and find them wanting, since God's ways are placed as far above ours as the heavens above the earth.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Skeptical theism reads this as direct support: we are in no position to judge that God lacks good reasons, given how far his thoughts exceed ours. The protest view answers that the same God who says this also invites lament and does not forbid the question, so the verse counsels humility, not silence. The cross-centered view adds that God's higher ways were revealed not by withholding reasons but by descending into the suffering himself.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Skeptical theism and the protest tradition together
biblicalEvidence.summary: God answers Job from the whirlwind with questions, not reasons: where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Job, the innocent sufferer, is given no theodicy, only an encounter with God's vast wisdom and Job's own limits.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for every theodicy that claims to supply the reason, since God supplies none to Job, and hard for a pure protest that demands answers, since Job is finally quieted not by an answer but by God himself.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Skeptical theism reads God's non-answer as confirming that Job, and we, are in no position to judge God's reasons. The protest tradition reads the book as vindicating Job's lament over his friends' theodicies, since God rebukes the friends who explained and not Job who protested. The cross-centered view reads the whirlwind as God giving himself rather than a system, the pattern the cross completes.

biblicalEvidence.summary: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? God in Christ cries the sufferer's own protest from the cross, entering godforsakenness, and quoting a psalm of lament, and receives no explanation in the moment.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any theodicy that answers suffering with a theory, since God's own response in the deepest suffering is a cry of why, not an explanation, and hard for a God pictured as distant from suffering, since here God is inside it.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The cross-centered view reads this as the center: God answers evil not by explaining it but by bearing it. The protest tradition reads the cry as divine warrant for lament, God himself crying the question. The free-will defense and soul-making views affirm the cross as the place where God redeems the evil that freedom and a hard world made possible, while granting that the cross is a deeper word than any theodicy.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The martyrs under the altar cry out, O Sovereign Lord, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? Even in heaven, the slain cry out in protest, asking how long, not yet given the full answer.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the view that faithful suffering must always be serene and unquestioning, since the redeemed in glory still cry how long, pressing God for justice.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The protest tradition reads this as decisive: lament and the cry for justice are not failures of faith but the voice of the faithful even in heaven, and God receives the cry rather than rebuking it. The skeptical theist notes the martyrs are told to wait, that the full reasons and timing are not yet given. The soul-making and free-will views read the eventual judgment as the resolution toward which the whole drama of a free, maturing creation moves.

weighing:
My judgment, offered tentatively, and with more unease than usual, because every theodicy I am about to weigh has at some point been used to wound someone I was trying to help.

On the logical and philosophical level, I think the free-will defense does real work and skeptical theism does more than it is given credit for. The free-will defense, in Plantinga's careful form, is enough to answer the charge that God and evil are contradictory, and I am grateful for it, because that charge needed answering and it has been answered. And skeptical theism, cold as it is, makes a point I cannot get around: the inference from this looks pointless to this is pointless quietly assumes we could spot God's reasons if he had any, and I see no grounds for that assumption in a creature as small and short-sighted as I am. So as defenses against the argument, against the claim that suffering disproves God, these two are the strongest tools we have, and I use them.

But here is where I have to be honest, and it is the crux of the whole page. A successful defense against an argument is not the same as a word you can speak to a sufferer, and the soul-making theodicy in particular tempts me to a cruelty I want to refuse. It is true, in the abstract, that hardship can grow a soul. It is also true that said to a parent at a child's grave, my child's death is making me a better person is something close to blasphemy. The theodicies work best at the desk and worst at the bedside, and the distance between those two places is where most pastoral damage gets done. So I find myself, with the protest and cross-centered tradition, increasingly convinced that the project of justifying particular sufferings should mostly be set down, not because the defenses fail logically, but because explanation is the wrong genre for grief. Ivan Karamazov returning his ticket has always seemed to me more reverent than the theodicist tidying the horror into a system.

So where do I land, tentatively. I keep the free-will defense and skeptical theism as defenses, for the doubter pressing an argument, and I would offer them in that setting. But for the sufferer, I put the theories down and reach for the two things the cross-centered tradition recovers: lament, which lets the wounded keep talking to God without pretending it is all fine, and the cross, where God answers evil not with a reason but with his own wounds. I cannot prove that is enough. I only know that a God who entered the suffering has comforted people that no theodicy ever reached. Hold the goodness of God, refuse to call evil anything but evil, use the defenses where arguments are being made, and at the bedside, mostly, be quiet, lament, and point to the cross.
charitableDisagreement:
The deepest disagreement on this page is not between the individual theodicies but between those who build theodicies and those who think the building is itself a mistake, and both sides are faithful, so handle the difference with care. If you are drawn to the cross-centered and protest tradition, as I largely am, do not despise the theodicists, because the doubter pressing an honest argument deserves an honest answer, and waving away every defense as cold rationalism leaves that doubter with nothing and can look like evasion. The free-will defense and skeptical theism have kept thoughtful people in the faith, and that is no small thing. And if you build theodicies, do not mistake a logical victory for a pastoral one, and never, ever carry your theodicy into a grieving home as though it were a comfort, because the same words that win a debate can break a heart.

The real test is the bedside, and it sorts the theodicies more honestly than any seminar. Ask of each: can this be said out loud to a suffering person without becoming a lie or a cruelty. The free-will defense, said gently and rarely, sometimes can. The soul-making theodicy almost never can, whatever its merits at the desk. Skeptical theism is honest but cold and lands as a shrug if offered too soon. The cross can almost always be offered, because it does not explain the suffering, it shares it. Let that test, not just logical strength, govern what you reach for and when.

So, is it a hill to die on. The goodness of God, yes, and the reality of evil as evil, yes, both first-order, both non-negotiable. But which theodicy you hold, or whether you hold one at all, is a second-order question that serious and compassionate believers answer differently. Defend God's goodness with everything. Hold your particular explanation of his ways with a light hand and a watchful eye on the cost of saying it, and remember that at the worst moments, presence has comforted where every argument failed.

relatedDebates.note: The theodicies are answers, and they only make sense against the question they answer. The logical problem, which the free-will defense addresses, and the evidential problem, which skeptical theism and the cross-centered responses address, are laid out on the problem-of-evil page, which also presses the honest weight that no theodicy fully lifts.

The cross-centered response depends entirely on whether God genuinely shares human suffering. If God is wholly impassible, only the suffering God can help needs careful statement; if God suffers, the comfort is immediate. The impassibility page takes up whether and how the God of the cross is moved by our pain.

relatedDebates.topic: Providence, freedom, and the open future
relatedDebates.note: What you can say about any particular tragedy depends on how God governs the world: whether he ordains all things, permits them, or works within a genuinely open future. The free-will defense leans on libertarian freedom, which connects directly to the foreknowledge debate among classical theism, open theism, and Molinism.
